I had a pretty good idea of what to expect when I started playing Orwell, but I was surprised time and time again about the absolutely amazing writing and the whole premise of the game. While not being overly complex in its mechanics, Orwell provides an emotional experience like few other games I have ever played and is able to capture the dystopian vibe of 1984 to an extremely disturbing level.

I started my first playthrough in the evening and it gripped me so much that I couldn't stop playing until I had finished the game some time around 3 a.m.

While the game doesn't offer a lot of choices, most of these actually do matter and then fold out in a logical way. Contrary to Telltale games, choices have an actual emotional impact on the player, which is something I haven't seen often in videogaming.

Everyone even remotely interested in storytelling and the workings of society should have played this to completion at least once. Especially people who think they have nothing to hide and don't see an issue with the paradigm of security above all. This game does actually successfully deliver a very disturbing perspective.

I remember clearly sitting with my dad looking at games to try, and we tried the demo for Orwell... I was blown away, what a brilliant idea for a game.

The story is amazing, the mechanics are intuative and easy to figure out, I got totally swept away by this game, and the message it has.
A good bit of replay value as you aren't able to get all information in just one run, and it pays off to look for it.
10/10 would recommend.

Although it has its flaws (a few times I was frustrated that some data chunks were "contradictory" although they could both be true, or that some information appeared only after I spent a minute agonizing over which similar data chunk is least incorrect), this is a very finely crafted portrait of surveillance and its moral implications. Even as someone pro-privacy and personal freedom, I found myself thinking "This is justifiable since it's for the good and safety of innocents".
Then the ending cutscene I got was about 30s long, yet somehow I'm still recovering.

Now, when I went into Orwell, I was fairly certain of what I would be getting out of my experience. An interesting little narrative set in an Orwellian-universe where you help figure out who perpetrated a terrorist attack. In a way, that's exactly what I got. But, looking back on my time with the game, I'm struck by how utterly wrong I was. Orwell exceeds all expectations and leaves me itching to either give the game another go, or threaten the developers at knife point to let me play Season 2, which the game helpfully reminded me to add to my wishlist before exiting the program.

I'm sure there's some connection that can be made to the game monitoring me in that last sentence, but I'll let it slide because Orwell deserves all the levity I can grant it.

Addressing the actual game instead of gushing all over my laptop and nearby furniture, it plays out as a sort of Point-and-Click adventure game where websites, conversations, and remote connections act as different areas, and datablocks act as items. The real twist is that, once you collect a new piece of information, there is no undo button. Your supervisor can only see what you let him see, and you can't take any information back if you realize you made a bad call or acted too hastily. And the game makes you live with it. After making a particularly blatant error, I fell back into bad habbits and attempted to quit the game and allow myself another go from whatever autosave the game keeps. 

Unfortunately for my inner gaming sins, Orwell knows exactly where you left off, as the exit screen likes to remind you. If you mess up, you've messed up permanently on that file. Wanna redo? Looks like you're starting over.

This knowledge that everything you do will have intentional and unintentional consequences makes this the most tense and nerve wracking narrative experience i've played in quite some time. This is especially apparent in the final act, which I won't be spoiling because everyone needs to experience the game's final twists and turns for themselves.

As much as I love the game, it isn't entirely without flaws. Some of the indicators for new information disappear too quickly, forcing me to search through articles trying to locate missing data. There are times where the information you need to use to progress the investigation is incredibly obscure, sending you on another hidden picture adventure. And, while I love the eavesdropping system, it can be somewhat tiresome to watch a conversation playout when you're dead set into 'Network Super Sleuth' mode and have to wait for dialogue to end before resuming the hunt. 

But all of those are nitpicks. The game is fantastic, and it makes me long for more games with this style of narrative/gameplay interaction. While I won't be playing through until I thoroughly forget some of the game's twists, rest assured I will be delving back into the world of The Party in the future.

I have been playing video games since the Atari 2600 and out of the many games I have played only 5  have inspired me to award them my own personal score of 10. Orwell has joined this very exclusive list for me. The game is a masterclass of using the medium of video games to make poignant social commentary that feels gripping and authentic. 

Daniel Marx (Game Designer) is a fantastic writer who gives each one of his characters a very distinct voice using colloquial dialogue and expressions that stay consistent for each character throughout the course of the 5 chapters of the story. His ability to create believable characters with personalities and motivations that feel real is the key to making the message of the game resonate. This isn't a simple story of noble heroes and evil villains, this is an examination of complex people and their struggles to reconcile their beliefs and their feelings, their fears and their ability to summon up the courage to do what they feel is right. 

The Gameplay is simple to understand, but choices made by the player do have branching consequences. Reminiscent of Telltale games and other members of the narrrative genre with a choice driven structure. The game manages to give the player a sense of real agency in the outcomes of the story, and have genuinley significant differences at several key moments. My mind spins at the challenge of writing a story that is able to stay consistent throughout its length, and yet offer a significant number of alternatives that need to be followed to their logical conclusion. Again, my compliments to Daniel Marx on his writing skills and game design. Impressive. Very impressive. 

The art style reminded me of the polygonal look of games like Out of This World and Flashback from the early and mid 90's with improved technology that looks good and yet remains accessible to all players even ones with 8 year old laptops (such as myself). Compliments to Melanie Taylor for an aesthetic that is easy on the eye and hardware. 

In the end, the writing, gameplay and art all serve to execute on making a statement about the ever increasing surveillance that is taking place in our own world and it is no suprise that the invasion of privacy that is possible at this very moment is something that can chill to the bone. We are at a crossroads in the story of humanity, whether the next chapters are dominated by the decision to sacrifice freedom for security or the acceptance that freedom carries risks, but is far better than a world where everyone is always suspect of being an enemy of the state and a target for elimination. 

Provided you do not object to reading a great deal (as there is no voice acting), this game will provide you with 10 hours of riveting narrative that will undoubtedly leave you questioning how much autonomy we are willing to surrender for the illusion of safety that a large surveillance state seemingly affords. 

I cannot recommend this game highly enough.

P.S. Additionally many thanks to Michael Kluge (Programming) for his coding work. The game runs very well. Amazing that this trio of developers crafted such a landmark title. I bow to your triumvirate of talent. 

P.P.S : Incidentally, in case anyone is interested, my other Perfect 10 games are :

- Legend of Zelda : Ocarina of Time
- Resident Evil 4
- Batman : Arkham City
- Last of Us
- Telltale's The Walking Dead : Season 1

This game is a lot of fun! I played the demo first to get a sense of the game, and believe me, the demo is just the beginning!

You play as an investigator who rakes through people's social media. phones, computers and news articles, taking lots of little snippits of information like their names, associates, attitudes about the government and issues, and report them to your higher ups in the government. It's up to you what to include or leave out (though some facts MUST be included to advance the plot). So you can show the social media post that's vaguely threatening toward the government or the one where the person is calling for reason and rejects hasty or violent behavior. How that person is treated under interrogation or at their arrest is up to you. As the name of the game implies, this is an Orwellian kind of nation, where "the greater good" means giving up some liberties in order for security, to the extreme. Choices matter, like informing the authorities where a person is going to be, whether they're armed. After I got one person killed, I started playing really close to the vest, not revealing information unless the story progression required it.

The story: It's interesting! There's a lot going on, never knowing who is behind the terrorist attack you've been called in to investigate. Some of the characters you end up investigating don't play into the story later (which is a waste), but the conflicting stories and attitudes keeps you guessing. There is a mechanic that lets you decide between two conflicting pieces of information, and it really puts doubt into you.

There's a little bit of replay value in that your choices matter, but a lot of those choices just end up with you just not arresting someone, or affecting the ending. There was one opportunity you have to prevent another terrorist attack, and I was really excited to try and parse through all the information but it turned out you never had enough info to begin with and just came down to a 50/50 guess. I guessed wrong, and people died. It doesn't seem fair, because the answer is obvious after you find out what is going on, but the game didn't allow you to investigate the person actually responsible BEFORE the event, so it really is just an uneducated guess. Missed opportunity for gameplay, in my opinion. You should get rewarded for scouring every document, not punished just because you weren't given the information.

Overall, though, Orwell is a fun experience. It raises a lot of highly topical issues about safety vs. security, about big data and surveillance and all that stuff. This isn't a dystopian future far removed from our reality. I can see this happening right here, right now. And that's why you should play this game.

Orwell is a short but engaging story about an investigator (that's you) being given incredible power to peer into the information of anyone you want. This idea does not seem far-fetched at all. In fact, despite its rather in-your-face name, Orwell presents a world that is quite believable. There really is nothing here that is overly dystopian or fantastic. Rather, the world in Orwell is just our own world, with surveillance taken a few notches up.

The game isn't perfect. The interface sure could use some work. I often found myself having to go through the same emails, chats, etc. until I found the link or "data chunk" it wanted. As such, it was a let down on its initial promise, and felt much more pre-determined than I hoped. There are a few choices here and there, but they don't feel like they matter much. In the end, things will go as they go, and there is little reason not to submit every data chunk.

All that said, Orwell is a good game, and well worth the time to play. It's not long - I did it in a single session. Hoping the sequel adds a bit more choice and complexity. But in a world where these type of games tend to go a bit too far in dystopian future, Orwell is very welcome, because it feels much closer to reality.  It clearly has a point to make, but it is generally not heavy-handed. Its most important trait is that it places you in the role of the investigator. You might find the level of access you have to be unnerving. But you feel like you're the good guy. In that way, it's both humanizing to the agents who pore through our data, and showing how no human should have that power.

Pick Orwell up. It'll be a few hours well spent.

I was really surprised by this beautifully designed (and beautiful looking) game that was both interesting and thought-provoking (no pun intended). 

In a world where we give our information up free of charge (this review included) it is increasingly obvious that the very information can be a) sold to the highest bidder and b) used against us. Whether in the name of 'security' or 'commercial ease' this game is a timely reminder that Big Brother is here.

George Orwell could only imagine the world we are now living in but he totally called it. 'Smart' devices that spy on us. Data miners and browsers that remember our every word. Governments that trump up charges to fit a political narrative (and I'm not just talking about 'dictatorships' but democracies too). 

Edward Snowdon proved a long time ago that technology, which we've all fallen in love with, has the power this game speaks so clearly about. Playing it really did give me chills as an Investigator for Orwell. I tried occasionally to do the 'right' thing and to out-manoeuvre the system, with pretty horrific consequences. That really added to the realism, as all information viewed out of context can be used to mean almost anything and fit any agenda required. 

I really enjoyed this game and I’ll definitely be running back through it again in the hope of outwitting The Man. I’m also seriously excited there’s going to be a sequel, which I can’t wait to play. This was some excellent work by the devs and a real pleasure to play!

Story is where the game really shines, however.  You play as the administrator to some Orwellian Big Brother type system used by the Government to spy on citizens suspected of Crimes (sort of a social media detective).  Tapping phone lines, e-mails, getting into people's personal computers, etc.  

I found myself becomming quite engaged by the characters, which is impressive if you consider you never have any direct intereactions with them besides spying on them.  Still as I went about my investigations I found myself feeling a nawing sense of guilt for violating the privacy of these characters to try and get at the Suspect I needed to catch.  That alone says something about the quality of the writing in the game.

I would highly recommend this game if you like a heavily story driven game, especially for only $10.  It's a unique experience that immersed me to the point where I was having actual emotional reactions to the story and characters.

TL;DR at the end.
     "Orwell" is like a choose your own adventure mystery novel mated with web browser of sorts. Unlike the trailer for this game, you do not spend any time viewing cctv footage or identifying and tracking people via facial recognition in the manner made familiar by television's "Person of Interest" or the popular "Watchdogs" game series. Its not like that. Its a look at what the internet, our PCs and social networking devices look like from the perspective of an invasive government investigation. It's got some tense moments that are done well but i've seen done better.
      If you have an interest in the themes of civil rights, criminal investigation and/or government corruption in the age of the internet (information age) you might like the game. The graphics are interesting and add to the personality of the game. The music is not memorable in itself, but musical cues when plot twists are revealed in the game are a nice and unexpected  touch.

Your advisor tells you pretty much everything you need to do and then like a cog in a machine, you just do it. 
There's a sorta hamfisted political message that it presents well and fairly subtly initally, but then fumbles towards the end of the game. It goes well with the story.
The one issue that I found to be pretty damaging with Orwell is that for such a story driven game, I didn't feel any emotions towards the characters. They're pretty average archetypes that are awkwardly written, as if one talented writer wrote the framework for the game and another less talented writer wrote the dialogue. The only real connection I formed was with the advisor character, which was just a shell for nearly 90% of the game, as a way to inject tutorial into the story without breaking immersion.

[h1]Big Brother Is Watching, and He Is YOU[/h1]

The premise of the game is simple. Instead of totally political or specifically relevant to George Orwell or his works, this game discuss about something that is very relevant to modern society: the surveillance. ORWELL gives you insights on how being able to supervise things doesn't warrant perfect surveillance. As reflected by the in-game quote, [i]you never really understands a person until you consider things from his point of view ... until you climb into his skin and walk around in it[/i]. And in its all complexion, it puts you in as the main actor to see how flawed things can be. 

[u][b]Gameplay[/b][/u]
The game puts you as the main actor, as "The Investigator". You have the ability to put [spoiler]or not to put[/spoiler] information to the surveillance tool, ORWELL. You will eventually confront the consquences on making the choices [strike]and regretting it.[/strike] [spoiler]although it didn't affect most of the plot, sadly[/spoiler]. You can make a difference for every piece of information you can get. For every piece of information, you can identify each suspects to narrow down informations and potentially prosecute them. However, you may never knew you might end up making choices that would actually provide faulty informations. But remember, not all information is essential in giving you the solution to the problems existing.

[u][b]Pros[/b][/u]
- Soundtrack that gives you chill
- Cool UIs
- Plot that shakes your moral values on surveillance by gradual changes
- An actual relevant plot
[spoiler]- I mean, you can take down SJWs in this game. It's a job you won't reject, no?[/spoiler]

[u][b]Cons[/b][/u]
- Short gameplay time
[spoiler]- Linear plot (until the end; your decision didn't matter for the end before the interview, no?)[/spoiler]

[u][b]Conclusion[/b][/u]
If you're not into the idea of surveillance, probably this game is a good introduction; or probably gonna be a bit boring if you really are into action. This game is about choices and identifying people in order to solve persisting issues. It has a plot that could give the players a shock through moral choices. It's replayable and enticing to figure out other ways to complete the game. Worth it's full price, but a must-buy when on sale.
